A few words to know

reconciliation

signatory

aggregate

tampering
Changing something dishonestly without permission.
follow-up reference
A code linking a later action to an earlier one.
underlying
Existing behind a summary or label.

04 · Read & review

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

Fiona's first message of the day contained a cautious but meaningful result. Several reference numbers in the recovered authorisations book corresponded to numbers in the payment-exceptions records. That supported the possibility that the volume belonged to the 2011 travel scheme, although it did not authenticate every page or establish that the approvals had been acted upon.

A clearer copy of the delegated-authority guidance had also been examined. It assigned certain exceptions to the finance manager and required requests above a threshold to go to the trust chair. The threshold figure was still partly unreadable, and the initials entered in the book had not been matched reliably to the people who held those posts.

“Malcolm Vale was chair,” Sarah pointed out.

“Which may tell us what he was authorised to approve,” Emma replied, “not which entries he actually signed.”

Fiona said her colleagues were checking contemporaneous staffing records rather than interpreting faint initials by guesswork. Emma welcomed the distinction. A plausible name was not the same as an identified signatory.

Later, an accounting summary offered a second route towards the money. It recorded monthly bank-payment totals but did not provide a list of identifiable recipients in the version that Fiona could discuss. No reconciliation with the individual approval references had yet been completed.

Sarah wanted to know whether the monthly total proved the grants were paid.

“It shows a reported banking total,” Emma said. “It doesn't connect a particular approved exception to money reaching a particular student.”

Emma reviewed Helen Ward's redacted letter. It said the cousin had been selected subject to further conditions; the family had not verified whether a transfer followed. Emma refused to search restricted records for a name to fill that gap.

The inspection report also resolved one source of suspicion. The loose leaf inside the authorisations book was still attached along one edge. The examiners had identified no missing sheet at that position. Emma crossed out the question removed page? in her notebook. Damage might be accidental, and the physical finding did not justify suggesting tampering.

Fiona agreed to request an independent comparison of staff authorisations and bank evidence, while warning that the surviving records might not support a complete reconstruction.

Towards evening she contacted Emma again. One exception entry bore a follow-up reference which also appeared in a banking index. The underlying transaction documentation had not yet been reviewed, and the code might indicate a correction, a returned payment or a completed transfer.

“Finally, one line we can follow,” Sarah said.

“One line we can test,” Emma corrected.

She wrote the reference in her notebook, without copying any student's identifying details. The prospect of a verifiable financial trail was more useful than the speculation that had surrounded the initials. But until the bank record was examined, the distinction between approval and payment remained intact.
